# Counit of Spectrum Adjunction is a Natural Transformation

**Theorem.** Let $\mathbf\Omega:\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Loc}$ be the locale-of-open-sets functor and
$\operatorname{Sp}:\mathbf{Loc}\to\mathbf{Top}$ the spectrum functor. Then the counit of the spectrum
adjunction $\sigma:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$, whose component at a
locale $L$ is the locale morphism $\sigma_L:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to L$ determined by the frame
homomorphism $\sigma_L^*:L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$, $a\mapsto\Sigma_a$, is a natural
transformation.

The claim is true; we prove it.

## 0. Conventions

**Frames.** A *frame* is a complete lattice $L$ (with bottom $\bot$, top $\top$, arbitrary joins $\bigvee$ and
meets) satisfying the frame distributive law
$$a\wedge\bigvee S=\bigvee_{s\in S}(a\wedge s)\qquad(a\in L,\ S\subseteq L).$$
A *frame homomorphism* $h:L\to M$ is a map preserving finite meets and arbitrary joins; "finite" includes the
empty meet, so $h(\top_L)=\top_M$, and "arbitrary" includes the empty join, so $h(\bot_L)=\bot_M$. Frames and
frame homomorphisms form a category $\mathbf{Frm}$ (identity maps are frame homomorphisms and composites of
frame homomorphisms are frame homomorphisms, so this is indeed a category).

**Locales.** $\mathbf{Loc}:=\mathbf{Frm}^{\mathrm{op}}$. Concretely: the objects of $\mathbf{Loc}$ are frames,
and
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(L,M):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frm}}(M,L).$$
For a locale morphism $f:L\to M$ we write $f^*\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frm}}(M,L)$ for the corresponding
frame homomorphism; thus $f\mapsto f^*$ is a bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(L,M)\to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frm}}(M,L)$, composition in $\mathbf{Loc}$ is characterised by
$$(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*\qquad (f:L\to M,\ g:M\to N),$$
and $(\operatorname{id}_L)^*=\operatorname{id}_L$. In particular two locale morphisms $L\to M$ are equal if and
only if the associated frame homomorphisms $M\to L$ are equal; this is the criterion we shall use throughout to
verify commutativity of diagrams in $\mathbf{Loc}$.

**The two-element frame.** $\mathbf 2:=\{\bot,\top\}$ with $\bot<\top$ is a complete lattice, and
distributivity is immediate by inspection (or: every finite chain is a distributive lattice, and all joins
occurring in the frame law are finite here), so $\mathbf 2$ is a frame. For $T\subseteq\mathbf 2$ we have
$$\bigvee T=\top\iff\top\in T,\qquad\text{and}\qquad x\wedge y=\top\iff x=\top\text{ and } y=\top. \tag{0.1}$$

**The functor $\mathbf\Omega$.** For a topological space $X$ let $\mathbf\Omega X$ be its set of open sets,
ordered by $\subseteq$. It is a complete lattice with $\bigvee\mathcal U=\bigcup\mathcal U$, finite meets given
by finite intersections, $\bot=\varnothing$, $\top=X$; the frame law holds because
$U\cap\bigcup\mathcal V=\bigcup_{V\in\mathcal V}(U\cap V)$ for sets. So $\mathbf\Omega X$ is a frame. For a
continuous map $h:X\to Y$, the preimage map $h^{-1}:\mathbf\Omega Y\to\mathbf\Omega X$ is well defined
(continuity) and is a frame homomorphism, since preimage preserves arbitrary unions and all intersections and
$h^{-1}(Y)=X$. We define $\mathbf\Omega h:\mathbf\Omega X\to\mathbf\Omega Y$ to be the locale morphism with
$(\mathbf\Omega h)^*=h^{-1}$. Since $(\operatorname{id}_X)^{-1}=\operatorname{id}$ and
$(h'\circ h)^{-1}=h^{-1}\circ h'^{-1}$, i.e. $(\mathbf\Omega(h'\circ h))^*=(\mathbf\Omega h)^*\circ
(\mathbf\Omega h')^*=(\mathbf\Omega h'\circ\mathbf\Omega h)^*$, the assignment $\mathbf\Omega$ is a (covariant)
functor $\mathbf{Top}\to\mathbf{Loc}$.

**Points.** A *point* of a locale $L$ is a frame homomorphism $p:L\to\mathbf 2$. Write
$\operatorname{pt}L:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frm}}(L,\mathbf 2)$, and for $a\in L$ put
$$\Sigma^L_a:=\{p\in\operatorname{pt}L:\ p(a)=\top\}.$$
We drop the superscript $L$ when it is clear from context. (Remark 5 below reconciles this with the
"completely prime filter" description of points.)

## 1. The spectrum functor

**Lemma 1.** For every locale $L$ the family $\tau_L:=\{\Sigma^L_a:a\in L\}$ is a topology on
$\operatorname{pt}L$. Moreover the map $\sigma^*_L:L\to\mathbf\Omega(\operatorname{pt}L,\tau_L)$,
$a\mapsto\Sigma^L_a$, is a surjective frame homomorphism.

*Proof.* Let $p\in\operatorname{pt}L$, i.e. $p:L\to\mathbf 2$ is a frame homomorphism.

*(i) $\Sigma_\top=\operatorname{pt}L$ and $\Sigma_\bot=\varnothing$.* Indeed $p(\top)=\top$ and $p(\bot)=\bot$
for every point $p$, by preservation of the empty meet and the empty join.

*(ii) Finite intersections.* For $a,b\in L$ and $p\in\operatorname{pt}L$ we have, using $p(a\wedge b)=p(a)\wedge
p(b)$ and (0.1),
$$p\in\Sigma_{a\wedge b}\iff p(a)\wedge p(b)=\top\iff\bigl(p(a)=\top\text{ and }p(b)=\top\bigr)\iff
p\in\Sigma_a\cap\Sigma_b .$$
Hence $\Sigma_{a\wedge b}=\Sigma_a\cap\Sigma_b$. Together with (i) (the empty intersection being
$\operatorname{pt}L=\Sigma_\top$) this shows $\tau_L$ is closed under finite intersections.

*(iii) Arbitrary unions.* Let $S\subseteq L$ and $a:=\bigvee S$. For $p\in\operatorname{pt}L$,
$p(a)=\bigvee_{s\in S}p(s)$, so by (0.1)
$$p\in\Sigma_{\bigvee S}\iff\bigvee_{s\in S}p(s)=\top\iff\exists s\in S:\ p(s)=\top\iff p\in\bigcup_{s\in S}\Sigma_s .$$
Hence
$$\Sigma_{\bigvee S}=\bigcup_{s\in S}\Sigma_s\qquad(S\subseteq L).\tag{1.1}$$
Now let $\mathcal U\subseteq\tau_L$ be an arbitrary subfamily and put
$$S:=\{a\in L:\ \Sigma_a\in\mathcal U\}\subseteq L .$$
(No choice principle is needed here: $S$ is defined by a condition, not by selecting one index per member of
$\mathcal U$.) Then $\{\Sigma_s:s\in S\}=\mathcal U$: if $s\in S$ then $\Sigma_s\in\mathcal U$ by
definition of $S$; conversely if $U\in\mathcal U$ then, since $\mathcal U\subseteq\tau_L$, we have
$U=\Sigma_a$ for some $a\in L$, and this $a$ lies in $S$ because $\Sigma_a=U\in\mathcal U$, so
$U\in\{\Sigma_s:s\in S\}$. Therefore, by (1.1),
$$\bigcup\mathcal U=\bigcup_{s\in S}\Sigma_s=\Sigma_{\bigvee S}\in\tau_L .$$
So $\tau_L$ is closed under arbitrary unions (for $\mathcal U=\varnothing$ this gives
$\varnothing=\Sigma_{\bigvee\varnothing}=\Sigma_\bot$, consistent with (i)).

Thus $\tau_L$ is a topology. Write $\operatorname{Sp}L:=(\operatorname{pt}L,\tau_L)$. By construction
$\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L=\tau_L$ is exactly the image of $a\mapsto\Sigma_a$, so $\sigma^*_L$ is
surjective onto $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$; and (i)–(iii) say precisely that $\sigma^*_L$ preserves
$\top$, $\bot$, binary (hence all finite) meets and arbitrary joins, i.e. that it is a frame homomorphism
$L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$. $\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.** Let $f:L\to M$ be a morphism of locales, with associated frame homomorphism $f^*:M\to L$. Then
$$\operatorname{Sp}f:\operatorname{Sp}L\to\operatorname{Sp}M,\qquad \operatorname{Sp}f(p):=p\circ f^* ,$$
is a well-defined continuous map, and $\operatorname{Sp}$ is a functor $\mathbf{Loc}\to\mathbf{Top}$.

*Proof.* *Well defined:* $p:L\to\mathbf 2$ and $f^*:M\to L$ are frame homomorphisms, hence so is
$p\circ f^*:M\to\mathbf 2$; that is, $\operatorname{Sp}f(p)\in\operatorname{pt}M$.

*Continuity:* every open set of $\operatorname{Sp}M$ is of the form $\Sigma^M_b$ with $b\in M$ (Lemma 1), and
$$(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M_b\bigr)=\{p\in\operatorname{pt}L:\ (p\circ f^*)(b)=\top\}
=\{p\in\operatorname{pt}L:\ p(f^*(b))=\top\}=\Sigma^L_{f^*(b)},\tag{2.1}$$
which is open in $\operatorname{Sp}L$. So preimages of open sets are open.

*Functoriality:* $(\operatorname{id}_L)^*=\operatorname{id}_L$, so $\operatorname{Sp}(\operatorname{id}_L)(p)=
p\circ\operatorname{id}_L=p$, i.e. $\operatorname{Sp}(\operatorname{id}_L)=\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Sp}L}$.
For $f:L\to M$ and $g:M\to N$ in $\mathbf{Loc}$ and $p\in\operatorname{pt}L$,
$$\operatorname{Sp}(g\circ f)(p)=p\circ(g\circ f)^*=p\circ(f^*\circ g^*)=(p\circ f^*)\circ g^*
=\operatorname{Sp}g\bigl(\operatorname{Sp}f(p)\bigr),$$
so $\operatorname{Sp}(g\circ f)=\operatorname{Sp}g\circ\operatorname{Sp}f$. $\blacksquare$

## 2. The counit and its naturality

By Lemma 1, for each locale $L$ the map $\sigma_L^*:a\mapsto\Sigma^L_a$ is a frame homomorphism
$L\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$, so it determines a locale morphism
$$\sigma_L:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\longrightarrow L .$$
This is the counit component (see §3, where we verify that this family is indeed the counit of the adjunction
$\mathbf\Omega\dashv\operatorname{Sp}$). Note that $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}$ is a functor
$\mathbf{Loc}\to\mathbf{Loc}$, being the composite of the two functors of Lemmas 1–2 and §0, and that
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ is a functor $\mathbf{Loc}\to\mathbf{Loc}$; so the assertion to be proved is
meaningful.

**Theorem.** $\sigma=(\sigma_L)_{L\in\mathbf{Loc}}$ is a natural transformation
$\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$.

*Proof.* Each $\sigma_L$ is a morphism $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to L=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}L$
in $\mathbf{Loc}$, as just noted. It remains to prove that for every morphism $f:L\to M$ of locales the square
$$\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L & \xrightarrow{\ \sigma_L\ } & L\\
\downarrow{\scriptstyle\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f} & & \downarrow{\scriptstyle f}\\
\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}M & \xrightarrow{\ \sigma_M\ } & M
\end{array}$$
commutes in $\mathbf{Loc}$, i.e. that
$$f\circ\sigma_L=\sigma_M\circ\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f
\qquad\text{as morphisms }\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to M. \tag{2.2}$$

Two locale morphisms $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to M$ are equal iff the corresponding frame homomorphisms
$M\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L$ are equal. Using $(g\circ h)^*=h^*\circ g^*$ twice, and
$(\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}f)^*=(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}$ by the definition of $\mathbf\Omega$ on
morphisms, (2.2) is equivalent to
$$\sigma_L^*\circ f^*=(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\circ\sigma_M^*\qquad\text{as maps }M\to\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L. \tag{2.3}$$

Let $b\in M$. On the one hand
$$\bigl(\sigma^*_L\circ f^*\bigr)(b)=\sigma^*_L\bigl(f^*(b)\bigr)=\Sigma^L_{f^*(b)} .$$
On the other hand, by (2.1),
$$\bigl((\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\circ\sigma^*_M\bigr)(b)=(\operatorname{Sp}f)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^M_b\bigr)
=\Sigma^L_{f^*(b)} .$$
The two agree for every $b\in M$, so (2.3) holds, hence (2.2) holds. As $f$ was an arbitrary morphism of
locales, $\sigma$ is a natural transformation. $\blacksquare$

## 3. Appendix: $\sigma$ really is the counit of $\mathbf\Omega\dashv\operatorname{Sp}$

For completeness we check that the family $\sigma$ described above is the counit of an adjunction
$\mathbf\Omega\dashv\operatorname{Sp}$, i.e. that each $\sigma_L$ is a couniversal arrow from $\mathbf\Omega$ to
$L$. (If one *defines* the counit abstractly through the adjunction, naturality is of course automatic; the
point of §2 is that the explicitly given family $a\mapsto\Sigma_a$ is natural, and the point of this appendix
is that the two descriptions agree.)

**Lemma 3.** For a topological space $X$ and $x\in X$, the map $\operatorname{ev}_x:\mathbf\Omega X\to\mathbf 2$
with $\operatorname{ev}_x(U)=\top\iff x\in U$ is a point of $\mathbf\Omega X$.

*Proof.* $x\notin\varnothing$ and $x\in X$, so $\operatorname{ev}_x$ preserves $\bot$ and $\top$;
$x\in U\cap V\iff(x\in U\text{ and }x\in V)$ gives preservation of binary meets by (0.1); and
$x\in\bigcup\mathcal U\iff\exists U\in\mathcal U:x\in U$ gives preservation of arbitrary joins by (0.1).
$\blacksquare$

**Lemma 4.** Let $X$ be a space and $L$ a locale. The map
$$\Psi_{X,L}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X,\operatorname{Sp}L)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(\mathbf\Omega X,L),
\qquad \Psi(h)^*(a):=h^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^L_a\bigr)\quad(a\in L),$$
is a well-defined bijection, and $\Psi(h)=\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h$ for all $h$.

*Proof.* *Well defined:* $\Psi(h)^*=h^{-1}\circ\sigma^*_L$ is a composite of frame homomorphisms
($\sigma^*_L$ by Lemma 1, $h^{-1}$ by §0), hence a frame homomorphism $L\to\mathbf\Omega X$, hence determines a
locale morphism $\mathbf\Omega X\to L$. Moreover
$(\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h)^*=(\mathbf\Omega h)^*\circ\sigma_L^*=h^{-1}\circ\sigma^*_L=\Psi(h)^*$, whence
$\Psi(h)=\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h$.

*Inverse:* define $\Phi:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(\mathbf\Omega X,L)\to
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X,\operatorname{Sp}L)$ by $\Phi(g)(x):=\operatorname{ev}_x\circ g^*$. This is a
frame homomorphism $L\to\mathbf 2$ by Lemma 3, so $\Phi(g)(x)\in\operatorname{pt}L$; and $\Phi(g)$ is continuous
because for $a\in L$
$$\Phi(g)^{-1}\bigl(\Sigma^L_a\bigr)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{ev}_x(g^*(a))=\top\}=\{x\in X:x\in g^*(a)\}=g^*(a),\tag{3.1}$$
which is open in $X$. Now:

- $\Psi(\Phi(g))^*(a)=\Phi(g)^{-1}(\Sigma^L_a)=g^*(a)$ for all $a\in L$ by (3.1), so $\Psi(\Phi(g))=g$.
- For $h\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Top}}(X,\operatorname{Sp}L)$, $x\in X$, $a\in L$:
$$\Phi(\Psi(h))(x)(a)=\operatorname{ev}_x\bigl(\Psi(h)^*(a)\bigr)=\operatorname{ev}_x\bigl(h^{-1}(\Sigma^L_a)\bigr)
=\top\iff x\in h^{-1}(\Sigma^L_a)\iff h(x)\in\Sigma^L_a\iff h(x)(a)=\top .$$
Since $\Phi(\Psi(h))(x)(a)$ and $h(x)(a)$ lie in $\mathbf 2$ and are $\top$ under exactly the same condition,
they are equal; as $a$ and $x$ were arbitrary, $\Phi(\Psi(h))=h$.

Hence $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ are mutually inverse bijections. $\blacksquare$

**Proposition.** For every locale $L$, the morphism $\sigma_L:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}L\to L$ is
couniversal from $\mathbf\Omega$ to $L$: for every space $X$ and every locale morphism
$g:\mathbf\Omega X\to L$ there is a unique continuous $h:X\to\operatorname{Sp}L$ with
$\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h=g$. Consequently $\mathbf\Omega\dashv\operatorname{Sp}$ with counit $\sigma$.

*Proof of the factorisation.* By Lemma 4, $\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h=\Psi_{X,L}(h)$ for every continuous
$h:X\to\operatorname{Sp}L$, and $\Psi_{X,L}$ is a bijection onto
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Loc}}(\mathbf\Omega X,L)$; so for each $g$ there is exactly one such $h$, namely
$h=\Psi_{X,L}^{-1}(g)=\Phi(g)$.

*Proof of the adjunction.* We use the standard characterisation of an adjunction by a counit (Mac Lane,
*Categories for the Working Mathematician*, IV.1, Theorem 2): given functors $F:\mathbf A\to\mathbf B$ and
$G:\mathbf B\to\mathbf A$ and a natural transformation $\varepsilon:FG\to\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf B}$
such that for every $A\in\mathbf A$, $B\in\mathbf B$ and every $g:FA\to B$ there is a unique
$h:A\to GB$ with $\varepsilon_B\circ Fh=g$, the assignment $h\mapsto\varepsilon_B\circ Fh$ is a bijection
$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf A}(A,GB)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf B}(FA,B)$ natural in $A$ and $B$, so
$F\dashv G$ with counit $\varepsilon$. Here $F=\mathbf\Omega$ and $G=\operatorname{Sp}$ are functors (§0 and
Lemma 2), $\varepsilon=\sigma$ is a natural transformation $\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to
\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ (Theorem of §2 — note that this is exactly where the naturality proved above
is used, and it is proved independently of the present appendix), and the required unique factorisation is the
statement just proved. Hence $\mathbf\Omega\dashv\operatorname{Sp}$ and the counit of this adjunction is
$\sigma$.

(For the record, the naturality of the bijection is immediate from what we have: for $k:X'\to X$ continuous and
$\ell:L\to L'$ in $\mathbf{Loc}$ one computes $\sigma_{L'}\circ\mathbf\Omega(\operatorname{Sp}\ell\circ
h\circ k)=\ell\circ(\sigma_L\circ\mathbf\Omega h)\circ\mathbf\Omega k$, using functoriality of
$\mathbf\Omega$ and the naturality square of §2 applied to $\ell$.)

Finally, taking $X=\operatorname{Sp}L$ and $g=\sigma_L$ recovers $h=\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Sp}L}$,
consistently with $\sigma_L=\Psi(\operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{Sp}L})$, which is the usual formula
"counit $=$ transpose of the identity". $\blacksquare$

## 4. Remark on conventions

Some presentations define $\operatorname{Sp}L$ using *completely prime filters*: subsets $F\subseteq L$ that are
upward closed, closed under binary meets, nonempty (equivalently $\top\in F$), do not contain $\bot$
(equivalently $F\ne L$), and satisfy: $\bigvee S\in F\Rightarrow s\in F$ for some $s\in S$. The assignment
$p\mapsto p^{-1}(\top)$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Frm}}(L,\mathbf 2)$ onto the set of
completely prime filters of $L$, with inverse $F\mapsto\chi_F$ (where $\chi_F(a)=\top\iff a\in F$); the frame
homomorphism conditions on $p$ translate exactly into the filter conditions listed, by (0.1). Under this
bijection $\Sigma_a$ becomes $\{F:a\in F\}$, and all statements above are transported verbatim. So nothing
depends on which of the two equivalent descriptions of points is used.

**Conclusion.** $\sigma:\mathbf\Omega\operatorname{Sp}\to\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf{Loc}}$ is a natural
transformation. $\qed$
